title: Who stopped being counted? COVID-19 case-reporting gaps across NZ sewer catchments, measured against wastewater and broken down by deprivation, 2022-2024
hypothesis: Across at least 50 NZ wastewater catchments with 30 or more weeks of paired data (Mar 2022 to Jun 2024), the catchment ascertainment index falls as catchment deprivation rises. The index is log weekly reported cases minus log flow- and population-normalised SARS-CoV-2 copies/person/day, with week fixed effects. Prediction: a 1-SD higher population-weighted NZDep2023 score goes with at least 15% fewer reported cases per unit of wastewater signal (multiplicative ratio <= 0.85, 95% CI excluding 1), after adjusting for sampler type (autosampler vs grab), log catchment population, % aged 65+ and region. Second prediction: the slope is steeper (more negative) after mandatory isolation ended on 15 Aug 2023 than in Mar 2022 to Aug 2023 (slope difference with 95% CI excluding 0). Either prediction fails if its CI includes the null or the estimate is on the wrong side of the threshold.
gap: Watson, Plank et al. (2024, Commun Med) combined NZ case and wastewater data to estimate one national time-varying case-ascertainment ratio, but they did not model differences between catchments. Overseas studies relate socioeconomic status to cases or wastewater levels in single cities or a few small towns (Georgia USA, Detroit, South Africa). None uses a national deprivation index, catchment-level case counts for 100+ sewersheds, and testing-policy breakpoints together. ESR/PHF Science released an unusual open resource: weekly reported cases aggregated to each sewer catchment, paired with the RNA series, for 134 sites from 2021 to 2024. It has not been used to measure who dropped out of case reporting as testing collapsed.
value_rationale: This fills a gap that is actively discussed: whether wastewater can serve as an ascertainment-independent equity monitor. The result would directly inform how PHF Science and Health NZ read case data in high-deprivation areas such as South Auckland, and how they size the reduced 12-site network and future pathogen panels (measles, influenza, H5N1). It is a new NZ-specific analysis, not a global open question, hence 6.
cost_rationale: All inputs are small tables (under 0.5 GB). Building approximate sewersheds from SA1 2023 polygons, the urban-rural classification and NZDep2023 takes about a day of GIS work. Panel regressions and sensitivity analyses run in minutes on CPU. No GPU is needed.
est_wall_time: 3-4 days (1 day data assembly and sewershed mapping, 1 day modelling, 1-2 days sensitivity analyses and write-up)

Novelty searches (OpenAlex: 'wastewater + Aotearoa', 'wastewater COVID-19 + New Zealand', 'wastewater + socioeconomic', 'wastewater SARS-CoV-2 underreporting socioeconomic', 'sewershed SARS-CoV-2 socioeconomic'; arXiv 'wastewater AND ascertainment'): found no catchment-level NZ deprivation analysis of case ascertainment
method: (1) Build a site-week panel from data_historic/cases_site.csv and ww_site.csv, plus data/ for the 12 sites still running to 2026. Compute AI = log(7*case_7d_avg + 0.5) - log(copies/person/day), dropping weeks below the limit of detection (500 gc/L floor) under a pre-specified rule. (2) Approximate each sewershed. Assign each WWTP to the Urban Rural 2023 urban area(s) it serves by name and nearest-plant matching, take the SA1s inside, and accept the mapping only if the summed 2023 usually-resident population is within +/-25% of ESR's catchment population. Multi-plant metros (Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch) use council-published catchment maps where available or are excluded from the primary analysis. (3) Covariates: population-weighted NZDep2023 score (z-scored), % aged 65+, log population, sampler type, region. (4) Primary model: linear mixed model AI ~ week fixed effects + zNZDep + covariates + (1|site), with cluster-robust SEs by site. Also fit a negative-binomial check on case counts with offset log(RNA load x population). (5) Period interaction: zNZDep x post-15-Aug-2023. (6) Sensitivity: autosampler-only sites; 0-1 week lag; leave-one-region-out; Omicron sub-lineage eras; excluding tourism/commuter catchments (e.g. Queenstown); a placebo that swaps in NZDep of adjacent unserved SA2s. (7) Descriptive extension: ascertainment trends 2024-2026 at the 12 remaining sites. Aggregate area-level data only.
plan: Download the ESR/PHF wastewater CSVs, NZDep2023 SA1 file, and SA1 2023 and Urban Rural 2023 layers (free Datafinder key); freeze checksums.
Build the site-week panel (cases, RNA, sampler type, population), apply the pre-registered LOD and minimum-weeks rules, and report the site count retained.
Map each WWTP to an approximate sewershed (urban-area SA1 sets) and validate against ESR catchment population (+/-25% rule); publish the mapping table and the excluded sites with reasons.
Compute population-weighted NZDep2023, % 65+ and rurality for each catchment.
Fit the primary mixed model and the negative-binomial check; test H1 (ratio <= 0.85 per SD NZDep) and H2 (steeper slope after 15 Aug 2023).
Run the sensitivity suite (autosampler-only, lags, leave-one-region-out, variant eras, tourism exclusions, adjacent-area placebo).
Describe 2024-2026 ascertainment at the 12 retained sites and estimate what share of the deprivation range the reduced network covers.
Write up the report with plain-language and equity framing; circulate to PHF Science and Northern region public health before release.
risks: Sewershed approximation error is the main threat. Catchment polygons are council IP, so mapping by urban area may misassign fringe SA1s; the population-match rule and the exclusion of metros limit this but reduce the sample. Cases are counted by residence while wastewater reflects where people are (commuters, tourists). Shedding varies by age, variant and vaccination. Flow normalisation errors (stormwater) and grab-sample noise affect small catchments. Policy dates must be fixed from official sources in the preregistration. Ecological inference: the result describes areas, not individuals. Te Mana Raraunga: the primary analysis uses only area-level deprivation. Any secondary use of Census ethnic composition stays aggregate and is framed as a health-system testing-access gap, not a property of communities, with no deficit framing. Findings should be shared with the Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards and Pacific health partners (e.g. Tāmaki Makaurau IMPB) before publication.
plain_summary: Sewage shows how much COVID is circulating in a town whether or not people get tested. This study compares sewage virus levels with officially reported cases in 50-100+ NZ towns and suburbs, to test whether poorer areas such as parts of South Auckland had markedly more 'missing' cases once free testing and isolation rules wound down. If so, case counts systematically understate illness where need is greatest, and wastewater could help correct that.
local_relevance: PHF Science and Health NZ's public health teams (including the Northern region covering Auckland) could use per-catchment under-reporting factors to adjust case-based alerts and to decide where the cut-down 12-site wastewater network, or future measles/flu panels, should sample. Auckland Council and Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards get evidence on where surveillance blind spots fall.

title: Forecasting NZ's 24-month childhood immunisation coverage from earlier milestones: a cohort-cascade model with a preregistered prospective test against the 95%-by-2030 Health target
hypothesis: In rolling-origin backtests over about 60 quarterly coverage releases (2012-2026; 20 districts; Total, Māori and Pacific groups), a cohort-linked cascade model beats two baselines at the 4-quarter horizon. The model predicts each birth cohort's 24-month full-immunisation coverage from the same cohort's earlier coverage at 12 months (observed 4 quarters before) and 6/8 months. The baselines are (a) persistence of the latest published 24-month coverage and (b) linear-trend extrapolation, and the model must have at least 30% lower mean absolute error than each (Diebold-Mariano p < 0.05). Prospective test: forecasts for the next two Health NZ quarterly releases (Q4 2025/26 and Q1 2026/27) are frozen and hashed before publication. For district totals they must achieve MAE <= 2.5 percentage points, with 70-90% of cells inside the 80% prediction intervals.
gap: NZ immunisation research is mostly descriptive or spatial (Marek et al. 2020 on 2006-2017 spatial change; Walls et al. 2023 on measles gaps; Rumball-Smith and Kenealy 2016 on the Northland pathway). Health NZ publishes each milestone's coverage separately every quarter, so the same birth cohort is visible at 6, 8, 12, 18 and 24 months in successive files, but nobody links these into a forward projection. There is no open, validated tool that says now where each district's 24-month coverage, the official Health target, will be in 12 months. Coverage has collapsed (6-month coverage 66.6% nationally and 48.5% for Māori in Jan-Mar 2026) and measles is spreading in NZ in 2025-26, so this tool is missing at an important time.
value_rationale: This is a constructive, actively needed tool. It gives an early read on progress to the 95%-at-24-months 2030 target, district and equity-group targeting 12-16 months ahead, and an input for measles immunity-gap planning during an active outbreak. The method is simple, and its impact depends on uptake by Health NZ, hence 6 not higher.
cost_rationale: About 120 small XLSX files (~50 MB total) are parsed into a tidy table. Hierarchical logistic or beta-binomial models with rolling refits take minutes to hours on CPU. Most effort goes into harmonising 15 years of changing file layouts and schedule definitions.
est_wall_time: 2-3 days for the backtest and frozen forecasts; prospective scoring when the next one or two Health NZ quarterly releases appear (expected within weeks to months)

lit_against: Marek L, Hobbs M, McCarthy JP et al. (2020) Investigating spatial variation and change (2006-2017) in childhood immunisation coverage in New Zealand. Soc Sci Med. doi:10.1016/j.socscimed.2020.113292 (descriptive spatial trends, no forecasting)

Novelty searches (OpenAlex: 'childhood immunisation coverage New Zealand decline', 'immunisation coverage forecasting cohort milestone', 'vaccination coverage nowcast forecast childhood district', 'Aotearoa Immunisation Register coverage', recent NZ immunisation titles 2023+): no cohort-linked coverage forecasting for NZ found
method: (1) Parse every quarterly file (2009-2026) into a tidy table of quarter x milestone x district x group (Total, Māori, Pacific, Asian, European/Other; NZDep quintiles) with eligible and fully-immunised counts. Harmonise DHB-to-district names and ethnicity labels ('NZ European' to 'European or Other'). Treat 'n/s' suppressed cells as missing and never back-calculate them. (2) Link cohorts: children reaching 24 months in quarter q reached 12 months in q-4, 6 months in q-6 and 18 months in q-2. (3) Cascade model: a beta-binomial/logit hierarchical model logit(C24[d,g,q]) = a[d,g] + b*logit(C12[d,g,q-4]) + c*catch-up[d,g,(q-4)] + period terms, with partial pooling across districts and groups. Catch-up is the recent cohort-specific gain from 12 to 24 months. Schedule-change breakpoints are explicit dummies (MMR moved to 12/15 months in Oct 2020, PCV changes, NIR-to-AIR migration 2023-24). (4) Rolling-origin evaluation uses only data published by each origin. Compare against persistence, linear drift and ETS baselines on MAE, weighted interval score and PI coverage, stratified by group and by era (stable pre-2020 vs 2020-2026 decline). (5) Freeze, timestamp and hash forecasts for the next two releases; score them on publication. (6) Report projected 24-month coverage per district to 2027 against the 95% target, and the projected measles-susceptible birth cohorts.
plan: Fetch all 2023-2026 Health NZ quarterly/annual files and the 109 archived 2008-2023 files via the Wayback CDX list; log URLs, capture timestamps and checksums.
Write a robust parser for the changing layouts (header offsets, ethnicity labels, district names); validate national totals against published headline figures.
Build the cohort-linked panel (milestone lags) and document schedule-definition breakpoints.
Fit the cascade model and baselines in a rolling-origin backtest (origins 2012-2026); compute MAE, WIS, PI coverage and Diebold-Mariano tests for H1.
Freeze the final model; publish hashed forecasts (with 80% PIs) for Q4 2025/26 and Q1 2026/27 before their release.
Score the prospective forecasts on release (H2); if only one release arrives within the study window, report it and append the second later.
Produce district x group projections to 2027 vs the 95% target and an equity-framed summary for Health NZ and Auckland's three districts.
risks: Schedule and definition changes (2020 MMR timing, PCV changes, the 2023-24 NIR-to-AIR register migration) break cohort comparability, so they need explicit breakpoints and sensitivity runs that exclude affected cohorts. Overlapping or rolling reporting windows and migration change the eligible denominators. Pacific and Māori cells are suppressed in small districts, so not all groups can be forecast everywhere. The prospective test depends on Health NZ's release timing. The archived files rely on the Internet Archive. Te Mana Raraunga: the study uses Māori and Pacific coverage data, published only as aggregates by Health NZ. Suppressed cells must never be reverse-engineered. Results are framed as the health system's delivery against Te Tiriti obligations (access and timeliness of services), not as whānau or community deficits. Outputs should be offered for review to Māori and Pacific immunisation researchers and to the Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards before release.
plain_summary: NZ's goal is for 95% of two-year-olds to be fully immunised by 2030, but coverage has dropped to roughly 80% or lower and measles is spreading. Babies who fall behind at 6 and 12 months tend to stay behind, so this project builds and tests a model that uses today's baby-vaccination numbers to predict each district's two-year-old coverage a year ahead. It will also make dated forecasts before the next official figures come out, so the model can be judged fairly.
local_relevance: Health NZ's immunisation programme, Auckland's three districts (Te Toka Tumai Auckland, Counties Manukau, Waitematā), Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards and Pacific providers could use the 12-month-ahead district and ethnicity forecasts to target catch-up outreach and measles readiness where the shortfall is predicted, instead of waiting a year for 24-month data.

title: Did ending ethnicity-inclusive surgical waitlist prioritisation in Auckland change who waits longest? A triple-difference evaluation around the Equity Adjustor Score (introduced Feb 2023, rollout halted Jun 2023, discontinued Aug 2024)
hypothesis: In Health NZ's monthly elective-surgery waitlist data, the outcome is the share of waitlisted patients waiting more than 120 days, compared between Māori+Pacific and European/Other patients. Prediction: in Te Toka Tumai Auckland this gap widened by at least 4 percentage points from the pre-controversy period (Jul 2021-Jan 2023) to the post-discontinuation period (Sep 2024-Jun 2026), relative to the same gap change in 15 districts that never used an ethnicity-weighted tool. The estimate is a specialty-fixed-effects, waitlist-size-weighted triple difference. Auckland's estimate must also rank first among all 16 districts in a placebo-in-district permutation (p <= 1/16). Negative control: the Asian minus European/Other gap, which the tool did not target, must show no comparable change (|estimate| < 2 pp). Disclosure for the preregistration: during feasibility checks the scout looked at raw, unadjusted quarterly gap series for six districts. The 4 pp threshold and the permutation and negative-control criteria are therefore set to be informative beyond that descriptive look.
gap: The tool caused a national political row in 2023. A Health NZ-commissioned expert panel (chair Prof Rod Jackson) judged it 'legally and ethically justifiable' but not best practice, and Health NZ dropped it on 1 Aug 2024 (RNZ). No public quantitative evaluation could be found of whether the ethnicity weighting changed ethnic inequities in waiting, or whether removing it reversed them. The only peer-reviewed NZ outcome study of a prioritisation tool covers Capital & Coast's non-ethnic General Surgery Prioritisation Tool (Wood et al. 2025). Health NZ now publishes monthly waitlist stocks by district x specialty x ethnicity from 2015 to 2026, which makes a credible quasi-experiment possible with open data.
value_rationale: The Auckland tool is among the most debated health-equity policies in NZ, and no outcome evidence has been published on it. A credible open-data evaluation directly informs Health NZ's promised national 'relook' at waitlist prioritisation and the Health target of 95% treated within 4 months. It also bears on Te Tiriti equity obligations. The design is a solid natural experiment rather than a global methods advance, hence 7.
cost_rationale: Five quarterly vintages of a ~5.5 MB XLSX (about 100k district x specialty x ethnicity x month rows). Regression, event-study and permutation analyses run in minutes on a laptop-class CPU. Hours to one or two days of work.
est_wall_time: 1.5-2 days (half a day data build and vintage checks, 1 day estimation, permutations and event studies, half a day write-up)

Cowan S, Waaka H, Wells C et al. (2025) Investigating postcode lottery: do regional outreach clinics improve waiting times to elective general surgical care for rural and Māori populations? Aust J Rural Health. doi:10.1111/ajr.70127

This is the closest work: a Capital & Coast tool without ethnicity weighting found no ethnic difference in booking odds, so it does not evaluate the Auckland ethnicity-weighted tool or its removal

Health NZ-commissioned expert panel review of the Auckland/Northland and Southern equity adjustor tools (chair Prof Rod Jackson; findings reported by RNZ, 1 Aug 2024). It assessed legality, ethics and robustness, but no public outcome evaluation was found

Novelty searches (Europe PMC: '"equity adjustor score" OR "equity adjuster"', 'waitlist AND prioritisation AND ethnicity AND New Zealand', 'waiting list AND Health New Zealand/Te Toka Tumai AND Māori/Pacific 2023-2026', 'algorithm/tool AND ethnicity AND surgical prioritisation AND New Zealand'; Crossref 'equity adjustor score surgical waitlist Auckland'; arXiv 'waitlist AND ethnicity AND prioritization'). No quantitative evaluation found. The OpenAlex daily quota was exhausted for this lead, so Europe PMC and Crossref were used instead
method: (1) Build a district x specialty x ethnicity x month panel (2015-2026) from the latest vintage. The outcome is long-wait share L = 1 - (waiting <120 d / total waiting). '<5' cells are handled as interval-censored (1-4) with bound-based sensitivity analyses. (2) Groups: Māori+Pacific (targeted) vs European/Other (reference); Asian vs European/Other as a negative control. (3) Treatment: Te Toka Tumai Auckland is primary. Waitematā and Counties Manukau are secondary or excluded because tool coverage is uncertain. Northland (later adopter, earlier stop) and Southern (own tool) are excluded from controls and analysed separately. Periods: pre-controversy Jul 2021-Jan 2023; tool era Feb 2023-Jul 2024, with a sub-split at the Jun 2023 halt; post-discontinuation Sep 2024-Jun 2026. (4) Primary estimator: a weighted (total waiting) triple-difference regression with district x specialty x group, specialty x month and district x month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by district, using a wild-cluster bootstrap because there are few treated clusters. Inference also uses a placebo-in-district permutation over 16 districts and a synthetic-control-style gap comparison. (5) Event study with monthly leads and lags to locate breaks at Feb 2023, Jun 2023 and Aug 2024, with pre-trend tests. (6) Specialty heterogeneity: general surgery, orthopaedics, ENT, gynaecology and others. (7) Data-stability check: quantify revisions to pre-period values across the five vintages. Aggregate published data only.
plan: Download all five waitlist-extract vintages; verify schemas and checksums; quantify vintage-to-vintage revisions for 2021-2024 months.
Build the analysis panel, compute long-wait shares by group, and fix the period and treatment definitions in the preregistration, recording the scout's descriptive peek.

Pin down the policy dates and which hospitals and specialties used the tool, using RNZ reporting and any Health NZ evaluation report or OIA release; record any uncertainty as alternative treatment definitions.
Estimate the primary triple difference, with wild-cluster-bootstrap CIs, and run the 16-district placebo permutation (H1).
Run the Asian-vs-European negative control and the event study (pre-trends; break timing at Feb 2023, Jun 2023 and Aug 2024).

Run sensitivity analyses: alternative treated sets (adding Waitematā and Counties Manukau), '<5' bounds, excluding outsourced high-volume specialties, unweighted estimates, and alternative long-wait thresholds where derivable.
Write a neutral, plain-language report with equity framing; offer pre-release review to Māori and Pacific health researchers and the Tāmaki Makaurau IMPB.
risks: Which hospitals and specialties used the tool, and when, is not fully documented in open sources. Moir (via RNZ) reports that Auckland weighted ethnicity 'for years' before the Feb 2023 five-factor algorithm, so the pre-period is not 'no weighting'; the estimand is therefore the effect of ending ethnicity-inclusive prioritisation. The long-wait share is a stock measure, so it also moves with referral and addition rates and with waitlist validation or removals, not only with scheduling order. Concurrent Auckland-specific shocks (private outsourcing in 2024-26, theatre capacity, industrial action) could confound, and specialty x month and district x month fixed effects only partly absorb them. With one primary treated district, inference relies on the permutation and bootstrap. Health NZ notes the data are live and revisable. The raw-data peek during scouting must be disclosed. The results will be used in a polarised political debate, so neutral wording is essential. Te Mana Raraunga: the study is centrally about Māori and Pacific equity. It uses only Health NZ's published aggregates, frames effects as properties of health-system prioritisation rather than of communities, avoids deficit framing, and offers findings for review by Māori and Pacific health leaders and the Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards before publication.
plain_summary: In 2023 Auckland hospitals used a scoring tool that gave some extra priority on surgery waitlists to Māori and Pacific patients, along with clinical need, time waiting, rurality and deprivation. After a political row the tool was stopped in August 2024. This study uses Health NZ's public monthly waitlist figures, compared with other regions, to test whether ending it left Māori and Pacific patients in Auckland waiting much longer than European patients.
local_relevance: Health NZ's planned national review of waitlist prioritisation, Te Toka Tumai Auckland surgical services, the Tāmaki Makaurau Iwi-Māori Partnership Board and Pacific health providers could use the estimates to decide whether, and how, equity factors belong in a future prioritisation tool. The evaluation code can then be rerun on each quarterly release.
